This was an excellent, thoroughly researched video.

I believe one of the main reasons Japan was never colonized was that the costs of conquering, occupying, and maintaining control over Japan outweighed the potential benefits of colonization. Although Japan had resources such as silver and copper, it was relatively resource-poor compared to China. Therefore, I think Western powers considered making profits through trade to be a less risky option.

Two major events that changed Japan's thinking were witnessing the conflict between Qing China and Britain and the shock of Commodore Perry's arrival in 1853. Seeing technologically advanced Western steam-powered warships firsthand created a profound sense of urgency among the Japanese: "If we continue like this, Japan will be destroyed!"

Since Japan was technologically behind the Western powers, it purchased battleships from Britain, including Fuji, Yashima, Shikishima, Asahi, Hatsuse, and Mikasa. Armored cruisers such as Asama, Tokiwa, Izumo, and Iwate were also built in Britain.

Japan also learned shipbuilding technology, naval gunnery, naval education, and fleet operations from Britain. Meanwhile, Japan drew heavily on French and German models for its army and legal system.

Thanks to these contributions, Japan was able to defend itself during the Russo-Japanese War. It is simply impossible to discuss Japan's modernization without acknowledging Britain's enormous contribution.

As for Japan's economic development after World War II, being forced to disarm ironically allowed the country to concentrate its resources on domestic reconstruction. In addition, the surge in demand for goods and services during the Korean War provided a major stimulus to Japan's economy, significantly accelerating its postwar recovery.

Yet, from the perspective of traditional East Asian civilization, Japan was historically nothing more than a barbaric pirate society associated with the infamous Wokou (倭寇). Until roughly 500 years ago, Japan was a backward society with no properly established government, plagued by internal warfare while its armed groups looted the coastlines of neighboring countries. In East Asia, Japanese people were derogatorily described as short, with unattractive teeth, and likened to a race of monkeys inhabiting an island nation. They were treated as fundamentally inferior. From the standpoint of orthodox East Asian civilization, the prevailing view was that Japan's history and culture were hardly recognized as an independent mainstream civilization in their own right.**

Japan, by contrast, followed the Western model and introduced a system requiring married couples to share the same surname, forcing wives to change their surnames to those of their husbands. In the eyes of traditional East Asians, this was nothing more than evidence of cultural backwardness: abandoning the very foundations of one's ancestral lineage in order to curry favor with the West.

@NyxelP-e3d 
I think you missed the central point of my argument, but here we go again.

Between the 1600s and the mid-1800s, Japan was largely isolated from the Western world, although it maintained limited trade with the Dutch, Chinese, and Koreans. Its military technology, including firearms, was not particularly exceptional compared with the industrializing Western powers. Japanese gunsmiths had learned to manufacture firearms after their introduction by Portuguese traders in 1543, but Japan subsequently fell behind major Western advances in military technology.

My argument is not that Japan lacked organizational capacity or the ability to modernize. It is that Japan's modernization cannot be separated from the geopolitical circumstances that allowed it to avoid the kind of colonial domination experienced by much of Asia.

By the nineteenth century, Western industrial powers possessed overwhelming naval and technological advantages. Had they considered the outright conquest or prolonged economic subjugation of Japan sufficiently valuable, they could have applied far greater military and economic pressure.

Of course, actually occupying Japan would have involved considerable costs, and successful colonization was never guaranteed. Nevertheless, the technological imbalance gave Western powers substantial leverage.

Japan was not entirely irrelevant strategically, either. Commodore Perry's expedition in 1853 demonstrated American interest in Japanese ports, trade routes, and potential coaling stations. But the Western powers largely pursued commercial access and unequal treaties rather than territorial conquest.

That distinction matters.

Japan's Meiji Restoration in 1868 was an extraordinary period of modernization, but much of its industrial, military, educational, and political development drew upon Western models. Japan actively imported foreign expertise, machinery, scientific knowledge, and institutional practices.

There is nothing inherently wrong with adopting foreign technology. Every industrialized civilization has done so. But portraying Japanese modernization as evidence of some unique national superiority ignores both Western technological influence and the geopolitical opportunities that made modernization possible.

China, meanwhile, faced a significantly different situation.

The Qing dynasty confronted devastating internal rebellions, political instability, the Opium Wars, unequal treaties, foreign-controlled treaty ports, and competing imperial spheres of influence. Western powers, and eventually Japan itself, exploited China's weakened political and economic position.

China also attempted military and industrial modernization, but its efforts unfolded amid enormous internal disruption and external interference.

Japan had greater opportunities to consolidate state power and direct resources toward industrialization without experiencing comparable territorial fragmentation.

Japan did not simply succeed because it was inherently more capable than China. The two countries faced different political, economic, and geopolitical circumstances. Geography, timing, institutional decisions, foreign competition, and historical contingency all mattered.

Ironically, Japan subsequently became an imperial power itself, acquiring Taiwan in 1895, annexing Korea in 1910, and expanding its aggression into China.

Now consider the Second World War.

Why did Japan attack the United States at Pearl Harbor in December 1941?

One major reason was its dependence on imported strategic resources, especially oil.

As Japan continued its military expansion in China and Southeast Asia, the United States imposed increasingly severe economic restrictions. In 1941, American financial sanctions and an effective oil embargo, alongside restrictions imposed by other powers, threatened Japan's ability to sustain its military operations.

Japanese leaders faced a strategic choice: abandon or significantly curtail their imperial ambitions, or attempt to seize the resource-rich territories of Southeast Asia.

They chose expansion.

The attack on Pearl Harbor was intended to neutralize the American Pacific Fleet while Japan pursued those territorial objectives.

That demonstrates precisely the vulnerability I am discussing.

Despite decades of industrialization, technological advancement, and military expansion, Japan remained fundamentally dependent on access to foreign resources and international trade.

Now imagine the consequences had comparable external economic pressure been imposed during the nineteenth century, before Japan established its modern industrial infrastructure.

Would Japan have modernized as quickly? Would it have developed the same industrial capabilities? Would its political institutions have survived such pressure unchanged?

Those are legitimate geopolitical questions.

It would be inaccurate to claim that Japan could never have developed advanced technology independently. However, it would be equally inaccurate to disregard how international trade, imported expertise, and access to raw materials accelerated Japanese industrialization.

As someone from Vietnam, a country that endured French colonial exploitation and fought for independence, I consider these distinctions important. Colonialism is not simply a question of military occupation. It also involves economic control, political coercion, unequal sovereignty, and the ability of a dominant power to constrain another country's choices.

That brings us to the American military presence in Europe and Japan.

American troops in Britain are stationed there under arrangements between longstanding allies. Germany's situation emerged from military defeat and Allied occupation following the Second World War. As the Cold War developed, American forces in West Germany became a central component of NATO's strategy to deter the Soviet Union.

Japan's postwar experience also began with military defeat, but the extent of American influence over its political reconstruction deserves particular attention.

Japan accepted UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER in 1945 and remained under Allied occupation, overwhelmingly directed by the United States, until 1952.

Its present constitution emerged directly from that occupation. The initial framework was drafted under General Douglas MacArthur's headquarters, although Japanese officials and legislators subsequently participated in revising and adopting it.
It was highly understand that it was the work of the American more than the Japanese to make sure the Japanese stop their racist superiority viewpoint against other Asian nation that set them on the course of war. 

Compare that with West Germany, where German representatives drafted the Basic Law under Allied supervision.

Both countries experienced foreign oversight, but the American role in shaping Japan's constitutional framework was exceptionally direct. 

Japan regained its formal sovereignty in 1952, but American military bases remained. Okinawa, in particular, continued under American administration until 1972.

Even today, the American military presence in Japan raises serious questions about sovereignty, jurisdiction, and the balance of power.

The Status of Forces Agreement establishes particular legal arrangements governing American military personnel. Japan retains legal authority, including criminal jurisdiction in specified circumstances, but disputes over jurisdiction, custody, military misconduct, and the burden placed on local communities have remained deeply contentious.

The history of Okinawa illustrates these tensions particularly clearly.

I am not arguing that modern Japan is legally an American colony. It is a sovereign state with its own government, institutions, economy, and foreign policy.

What I am arguing is that formal sovereignty does not automatically eliminate structural dependency or unequal power relationships. 

A military alliance can provide genuine mutual benefits while still reflecting a profound imbalance in geopolitical influence.

That is why I question the tendency to explain Japan's historical development primarily through cultural characteristics such as discipline, hierarchy, or organizational efficiency.

Those factors may have contributed to its development, but they cannot explain the larger geopolitical conditions under which Japan industrialized, expanded its empire, suffered military defeat, and subsequently rebuilt under American influence.

Japan's achievements are real. So are China's, and so are those of other societies that experienced very different historical circumstances.

But none of these achievements exists independently of history.

My argument is not that Japan was incapable of modernization. My argument is that Japan's success was shaped by opportunities, external influences, and geopolitical circumstances that were not equally available to other Asian countries.

To ignore that history and attribute the outcome mainly to cultural superiority is to confuse historical advantage with inherent superiority.

And that is precisely the distinction I am making.

The Chinese mainland has historically been a region where Han and non-Han peoples fought struggles for survival and dominance. The first period in which China came under the rule of a non-Han people was during the Sui dynasty.
